Since then, keeping track of everything has just become harder and harder.\n\nDoctor: Because of your memory problems, have you ever gotten lost in a familiar place, left the stove on, missed paying important bills, or taken the wrong medicines in a way that put your safety at risk? Or is it mostly forgetfulness and disorganization without those major problems?\n\nPatient: No, fortunately I have never gotten lost or left the stove on, and I haven't had any dangerous medication mix-ups. It is really just everyday forgetfulness and disorganization, like missing my daily vitamins or forgetting to bring my supplies to quilting meetings.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone close to you, like your daughter or friends at church, clearly noticed that your memory or organization has worsened compared with a couple of years ago? If so, what changes have they pointed out?\n\nPatient: Yes, sadly, others have definitely noticed and it has been quite embarrassing. People at church and in my volunteer groups have stopped relying on me for important tasks because of my constant mix-ups, and my daughter now double-checks my plans because she's worried I'll forget the grandkids' schedules.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told by a doctor that your memory problems are due to a medical or brain condition, such as a stroke, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, or another neurological illness? When I brought up these memory struggles with my primary care doctor, they didn't find a physical cause and recommended this psychiatric evaluation to look into underlying attentional issues instead.\n\nDoctor: Do you mainly lose track because your mind drifts and you have trouble focusing in the moment, or do you feel you pay attention fine but still cannot remember the information later? Since then, keeping track of everything has just become harder and harder.\n\nDoctor: Because of your memory problems, have you ever gotten lost in a familiar place, left the stove on, missed paying important bills, or taken the wrong medicines in a way that put your safety at risk? Or is it mostly forgetfulness and disorganization without those major problems?\n\nPatient: No, fortunately I have never gotten lost or left the stove on, and I haven't had any dangerous medication mix-ups. It is really just everyday forgetfulness and disorganization, like missing my daily vitamins or forgetting to bring my supplies to quilting meetings.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone close to you, like your daughter or friends at church, clearly noticed that your memory or organization has worsened compared with a couple of years ago? If so, what changes have they pointed out?\n\nPatient: Yes, sadly, others have definitely noticed and it has been quite embarrassing. People at church and in my volunteer groups have stopped relying on me for important tasks because of my constant mix-ups, and my daughter now double-checks my plans because she's worried I'll forget the grandkids' schedules.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told by a doctor that your memory problems are due to a medical or brain condition, such as a stroke, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, or another neurological illness? Or has no clear medical cause been found?\n\nPatient: No, I've never been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions like a stroke or Parkinson's. When I brought up these memory struggles with my primary care doctor, they didn't find a physical cause and recommended this psychiatric evaluation to look into underlying attentional issues instead.\n\nDoctor: Do you mainly lose track because your mind drifts and you have trouble focusing in the moment, or do you feel you pay attention fine but still cannot remember the information later? Can you give one recent example?\n\nPatient: It is definitely more that my mind drifts off and I lose focus in the moment, rather than just forgetting things later. For instance, when I sit down to read the notes from our garden committee or follow a Bible study lesson, my mind will wander after just a few minutes and I'll realize I’ve completely missed half of what I was reading.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you already have similar problems with attention, distractibility, or disorganization at school, work, or home? Or did these difficulties only begin later in adulthood?\n\nPatient: Yes, these difficulties actually go back to when I was a young girl in grade school. My teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but \"daydreamed too much\" and forgot to turn in homework I had already finished. I also talked out of turn so much that they had to move my seat more than once.\n\nDoctor: Do these attention and organization problems happen in several parts of your life, like at home, in social activities, and in past jobs or school, rather than only since retirement? Can you give one example from adulthood before the last two years?\n\nPatient: Yes, they currently affect multiple areas, from forgetting my pills at home to messing up my volunteer and church commitments. However, during my adult working years prior to these last two years, I didn't really struggle because my job had a very rigid, clear structure. Back then, I actually had a reputation for being incredibly organized and reliable, so this is quite new for my adulthood.\n\nDoctor: Before retirement, even if your job structure helped, did you still need unusual effort, strict routines, or reminders to manage attention and organization in daily life? Or did these problems truly disappear for most of your adult years and only return in the last two years?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about it that way. I think I just did what I had to do to keep up with my work back then, and having a busy, set routine seemed to keep me on track without me realizing it. It didn't feel like an unusual effort at the time.\n\nDoctor: Outside of your structured job years, did you continue to have lifelong problems with things like losing items, forgetting appointments, procrastinating, or being easily distracted at home or in other settings? It is really just everyday forgetfulness and disorganization, like missing my daily vitamins or forgetting to bring my supplies to quilting meetings.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone close to you, like your daughter or friends at church, clearly noticed that your memory or organization has worsened compared with a couple of years ago? If so, what changes have they pointed out?\n\nPatient: Yes, sadly, others have definitely noticed and it has been quite embarrassing. People at church and in my volunteer groups have stopped relying on me for important tasks because of my constant mix-ups, and my daughter now double-checks my plans because she's worried I'll forget the grandkids' schedules.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been told by a doctor that your memory problems are due to a medical or brain condition, such as a stroke, Parkinson’s disease, seizures, or another neurological illness? Or has no clear medical cause been found?\n\nPatient: No, I've never been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions like a stroke or Parkinson's. When I brought up these memory struggles with my primary care doctor, they didn't find a physical cause and recommended this psychiatric evaluation to look into underlying attentional issues instead.\n\nDoctor: Do you mainly lose track because your mind drifts and you have trouble focusing in the moment, or do you feel you pay attention fine but still cannot remember the information later? Or did these difficulties only begin later in adulthood?\n\nPatient: Yes, these difficulties actually go back to when I was a young girl in grade school.
